title: $18.54M for a Ferrari Daytona SP3 Is Crazy, But So 2026

body_markdown: Another week, another brightly colored Ferrari sold for eye-watering money. Prancing horses at crazy prices have been one of the few consistent themes of 2026. We’ve touched on it a lot and are almost tired of talking about it, but a Daytona SP3 for eight figures is still worth taking some time to discuss, and while few segments of the market are booming, this one is and it’s booming the loudest. The lovely green hypercar in question sold for[$18.54M](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/lv26_r0073/2025-ferrari-daytona-sp3) , many times as much as its one and only owner paid for it, and nearly $9M than another brightly hued SP3 sold for on the very same day. What gives? Broad Arrow Ferrari first started building the Daytona SP3 in 2022. The second in the company’s “Icona” lineup of limited-edition models that began with the Monza SP, it takes its name, layout, and some of its styling cues from the 330 P3/P4 and 412P that swept the top three places at the 24 Hours of Daytona in 1967. The engine is a bit old school, too: a big V-12 with no turbos, no hybrid systems, and horrible fuel economy (13 combined mpg). The 6.5-liter mill boasts titanium pistons, cams, connecting rods, and valves, and it makes 829 horsepower at a wailing 9250 rpm. Ferrari sold 600 examples to pre-selected customers, making the SP3 rare but not insanely so. It is rarer than a[LaFerrari](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+laferrari) (710 built), but more common than an[Enzo](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+enzo) (400 built) and an[F50](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+f50) (349 built). Broad Arrow The lucky New York collector/customer who bought this one specified a bespoke shade of *Verde Francesca* , which reportedly added $42,185 to the bill. The lower bodywork, front splitter, side sills, lid lip, and roof are all finished in bare carbon fiber, with most of the interior in Nero Alcantara but the seats and door panel padding in something called “Mustard Aunde Jeans.” Built in October 2024, it also came with nifty little extras, like a 1:8-scale Amalgam model of the car, a special red leather backpack and duffle bag, two pairs of driving gloves, a storage bag for the removable roof, and a window sticker. That window sticker reads a total suggested retail price of $2,334,048, a number of little relevance in today’s market, even though the date on that sticker is 2025. We added SP3s to our price guide earlier this year, and the condition #1 (best in the world) value is $16M after several huge sales in 2026 (one sold for[$26M](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo25/lots/r0035-2025-ferrari-daytona-sp3-tailor-made/) last year, but that was for charity). We’ll be raising that value after this sale, which took place at Broad Arrow’s Las Vegas Auction on October 31 and saw 64 lots sell out of 84 offered, for a grand total of $92.8M. About 40% of that total was down to just two cars, a 106-mile Ferrari F50 for a record[$18.705M](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/lv26_r0080/1997-ferrari-f50) , and this green SP3. The $18.5M paid for it is even more surprising when you look across the pond at another SP3 sold at the RM Sotheby’s auction in London. It sold for[£8,161,25](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/lf26/lots/r0063-2022-ferrari-daytona-sp3/) (about $10.9M) on the very same day. Alex Penfold/RM Sotheby's Broad Arrow The nearly $9M gulf between the two cars is a surprisingly huge one, but not an arbitrary one. The London car’s *Giallo Triplo Strato* paint is appropriately loud, but it’s not as unique as the *Verde Francesca* on the Vegas car. The London car was also a development and press car, so it was flogged by journalists from *Top Gear* , *Motor Sport* , *Car and Driver* , and *Road & Track* . As a result, its odometer reads 2948 miles, which is barely broken in on most cars but a fairly high figure on a nearly new Italian hypercar. The Vegas SP3, meanwhile, shows just 81 miles. Collector exuberance for rare-color, no-mile exotics is also generally higher right now in the U.S., where the green car sold, than it is in the U.K., where the yellow one did. Indeed, now more than ever, the rarest specs, rarest colors, lowest miles, and most exceptional condition can add up to millions in price difference at this level of the collector car market. This sale has us wondering, in the longer term, how sustainable this trend is (and after everything on the stock market this week, maybe not very). Not just how many “instant collectibles” can multiply in value over a few months, but also how many brilliantly engineered driving machines will be most prized when nobody drives them at all, and how much some of the little details will matter. Will the high-end collectors of 2046 or 2056 still prefer, to the tune of millions, a unique color and a two-digit odometer reading in the Vegas car over factory development history and high-profile period press appearances in the London one? After all, historical significance and cultural relevance are what have traditionally made cars collectible, not minutiae and manufactured exclusivity. That’s for the future to decide, however. For now, the bidders want uniqueness above all else, and they’re showing it with their paddles.
